en: The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states that when the Vinaya does not permit [certain matters], [the practitioner] gives rise to [joy]. ...
[He] rejoices with celebration. Anuruddha, foremost in the divine eye, [beheld] the marks of the devas.
"O Eye,
we wish to hear it; therefore,
we look upon you with joy."
Regarding "seeing all Buddha-lands": previously one saw three thousand [worlds], but now one beholds my Buddha-land;
[the mind] is unable to take conditioned existence as its object.
While existence cannot be contemplated as empty,
it is only when one clearly realizes that the Tathāgata is devoid of both the marks of existence and non-existence that one truly perceives all phenomena.
Those referred to as Upāli are those who uphold the Vinaya.
He is worthy of being asked about his illness;
it is for this reason that I have sent him.
This man has reached a point where he dwells in unwholesome states; therefore, I rebuke him so as to provide a means for the removal of his transgressions.
"As for not daring to question the Buddha:
while the Tathāgata was in the world, I was so overcome by shame and trepidation that I did not dare to question the Buddha;
I have come now to question Upāli."
As one who speaks according to the Dharma, I shall explain what I have understood in my own mind: the origins of offenses, their future retributions, and the methods for their eradication.
It is for this purpose that I speak to you with this staff.
"Directly eliminate it without disturbing the mind" means that for those who explain the characteristics of transgressions,
one eliminates these crookednesses and removes their increasing delusion;
alternatively, by directly explaining emptiness, one may eliminate their transgressions.
Therefore, it is said that one should simply eliminate [the afflictions] without disturbing the mind. Why is this so?
Why is it that by directly contemplating emptiness, one is able to eliminate transgressions?
The following clarifies that because offenses are empty, they can be eliminated.
"Not within" means that the offense does not reside in one's own person.
That which does not exist externally refers to the absence of weapons, staves, and so forth among sentient beings.
Since it does not exist in these three locations, one knows that there is no offense.
Because the following four aggregates (*skandha*) are empty, one realizes emptiness.
Regarding "defilement of the mind":
the mind is a real dharma, yet sentient beings receive the designation "defiled."
Thus we know that defiled phenomena are not fixed;
the luminous mind is likewise so.
That the mind is also not internal—
Clearly understand that the aggregates are empty.
That which resides within the sense faculties is internal;
that which does not reside within the external objects is external.
"It does not abide in emptiness, nor in conditioned phenomena, nor in between them.
As it is with the mind, so it is with the stains of transgression;
this clarifies that because the mind does not abide in these three locations, it is empty.
Since sin does not depart from the mind and the essence of the mind is empty,
how could there be sin?
The very essence of sin is emptiness.
Therefore, it is said that "the stains of transgression are likewise,
and all phenomena are likewise," meaning they are identical in kind to the emptiness of all phenomena.
"Is there, then, any defilement?
[The Buddha] countered Upāli with this question:
"All are entirely empty of mental characteristics."
"One does not see its defilement;
the mental characteristics of all sentient beings are likewise without defilement."
This constitutes the emptiness of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Regarding "deluded thoughts are defilements":
because deluded thoughts give rise to many views, they are called defilements.
This clarifies that the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is empty.
Regarding "perversion is defilement":
this [aggregate of] feeling (vedanā) is called "defilement" because it gives rise to afflictions (kleśa).
This clarifies that the aggregate of sensation is empty;
the grasping at a self is defilement.
This clarifies that the aggregate of formations is empty.
This is precisely the essence of defilement (*saṃkleśa*).
The first three [categories] are called "defilements" because they are able to produce defilement.
From the passage "all phenomena arise and perish" onwards...
This provides an extensive explanation of offenses and the emptiness of the four aggregates.
One knows they are empty because they arise and perish without abiding, being like illusions, transformations, and so forth.
This is called one who upholds the Vinaya.
If one can act as explained above, they are truly one who upholds the Vinaya;
the same applies to one who understands it well.
The reason for summoning Rāhula was that he,
being foremost in upholding the precepts, was capable of inquiring after the illness;
therefore, he was summoned.
Rāhu had nearly lost his way; for those who are at the root of the path,
one should hear of the signless renunciation and immediately explain for them the benefits and merits of renunciation.
Some say there is the benefit of having signs;
one should not speak of the benefits of the merit of leaving the household life,
nor should one speak of the benefit of having signs.
Why is this so? Why should it not be said that there is benefit in signs?
This is because one is a renunciant.
It clarifies that those who come before [the Buddha] should hear of renunciation through signlessness (*animitta*).
Within signlessness, there are no signs or benefits;
because there is no merit, it is said to be "without merit."
Now, regarding those who have left the household life:
the minds of such ordinary persons should hear that there is no benefit and no merit in leaving the household life.
As for the statement that "there is no self, other, or what is between them," it means this.
The reason this text was composed is to clarify that emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the source of all phenomena;
by attaining mastery over the principle of emptiness, all phenomena can be established.
The *Madhyamaka-śāstra* states:
"Because emptiness exists, all phenomena are established.
The *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* states:
Because it possesses the profound meaning of the great divisions, it accomplishes the six pāramitās;
thus, emptiness is the foundation of all phenomena.
Without it, there is no nirvāṇa.
Without this, there is no birth and death;
in the interim,
there is no Eightfold Noble Path.
Since these three do not exist,
all phenomena are thus empty;
emptiness is the source of all phenomena.
The following section on "being free from the sixty-two views" clarifies that emptiness has extensive accomplishments.
As for "being free":
Because it clarifies that these do not exist, one attains liberation from all bases of views.
As for nirvāṇa, because it clarifies that those do not exist, one attains nirvāṇa.
It is that which is accepted by the wise;
because it is clearly understood to have no interval, it is accepted by the wise.
As for "subduing the various māras":
He caused Māra to renounce the world;
Māra attained the five eyes and so forth.
Originally, Māra was characterized by affliction, confusion, and evil.
Now, having departed from afflictions and evil,
he subdues the non-Buddhists and leads those who have gone forth among the non-Buddhists.
One who transcends conventional designations transforms those sentient beings into emptiness; since sentient beings are already empty, [they are thus transformed].
Because one is unstained by conventional designations,
it is said that one has emerged from the mud.
Having emerged from the mire, one is no longer bound by conventional designations.
Therefore, it is said that there is no attachment.
From the phrase "no sense of 'mine'" (*amama*) onwards,
the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is clarified.
Not maintaining the five aggregates is called "no-self.
Not admitting sensory objects is called "having no reception.
To depart from all evils by following meditative concentration—
The phrase "superiorly departing from evil" clarifies all evils;
this "departing from evil" clarifies the evil that obstructs emptiness.
The reason for addressing Ānanda is as follows:
At that time, people thought that only those who were widely learned could inquire after the illness;
thus, he was summoned. His error lay in his failure to understand the Way, for he believed that one who has attained the ultimate truth could still be ill.
This section consists of three parts.
The first clarifies that the Dharmakāya is free from illness;
the second begins with "Stop, stop" and extends to "having heard these words."
Having severed all evils and fully perfected all virtues,
how could there be illness?
Within this, the preceding section contains two meanings.
Preface: When those of young body fall ill, they should use cow’s milk;
now, it is again used to bring about cessation through two stages.
Li! In the past...
Regarding the statement that the Tathāgata Riva was ill,
from "the wheel-turning [king]" downwards,
the second section clarifies the use of lower instances to illustrate higher ones.
"O Ānanda, go! Go quickly and depart, for you shall witness the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body free from ailment."
It should be understood that from here downward, the text clarifies the severance of evil and the sufficiency of goodness;
it clarifies that the Dharma-body is free from affliction.
From this point onward, it clarifies that the Tathāgata does not fall within the categories of conditioned phenomena.

In the "Bodhisattva Chapter," how could it be appropriate for Maitreya, the Bodhisattva who is the successor to the position of Buddhahood,
to manifest such a display of submissiveness?
It would not suffice to demonstrate the sublime virtue of Vimalakīrti.
This was spoken for the sake of the King of the Tuṣita Heaven regarding the practice of non-retrogression.
It clarifies that when the devas heard that Maitreya would be born there, a sense of joy arose within them;
therefore, they inquired about the practice of non-retrogression of the ten stages.
Vimalakīrti rebuked them to dispel the celestial beings' attachments;
he taught this for the sake of those practicing non-retrogression,
clarifying that these devas rejoice in such conduct and thereby attain bodhi and nirvāṇa.
Because one remembers this fruit, and because the attainment of the fruit arises from the cultivation of the resolve for enlightenment (bodhicitta),
each of these pure qualities is not [identical to] those five matters.
As for the question of which [state of] mind to employ,
the minds are simply too numerous.
It is difficult to grasp even one mind, let alone maintain mindfulness of them all.
Regarding the question of whether they are past, future, or present:
this clarifies that a single moment of mind is conceived as three [moments] existing within the three periods of time;
therefore, it is definitively stated that they are past, future, and present.
Regarding those whose past births have already ceased:

is it not that because the past mind has already ceased, one cannot receive a prediction? Regarding those whose future births have not yet arrived: [is it not that because the future mind does not yet exist, one cannot receive a prediction?]
That which has not yet arrived is a future non-existent dharma;
it cannot be designated.
That which is present does not abide.
Mindfulness is established through three characteristics; as each moment of thought does not abide, it cannot be designated.
In these three locations, the mind is absent.
"Where is that record? [The opponent asks.
"That which arises, ages, and ceases at this very moment" refers to citing the Buddha’s words as proof that a single thought-moment possesses the three characteristics.
The objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) exists throughout the three periods of time.
That which cannot [be said to] arise is the characteristic of arising (jāti-lakṣaṇa).
That which is old is the characteristic of abiding (sthiti-lakṣaṇa).
"Cessation" refers to the characteristic of cessation.

The text states: "If one were to [apply] 'non-arising' up to 'unsurpassed perfect enlightenment'... within emptiness, one cannot even obtain a prediction; it is not that one destroys enlightenment, but rather that one destroys the prediction."
The prediction regarding Bodhi is because it accords with [the ultimate reality];
as for those who receive a prediction upon birth, they did not obtain that prediction within the previously explained state of emptiness.
This trace receives its prediction within emptiness;
emptiness should be that which receives the prediction.
Now it is clarified that, because there is no arising or ceasing within emptiness, [it is so].
What is the significance of this prediction? Why is it so?
And why is it that when Maitreya receives his prediction, all sentient beings receive it together with him?
Now, that which is "suchness" (tathatā) is neither dual nor differentiated.
Sentient beings and Maitreya are equally suchness and non-dual;
furthermore, there is no distinction between Maitreya receiving a prediction of enlightenment and sentient beings not receiving it.
Since emptiness is without distinction,
one should attain it equally.
Second, from "If Maitreya attains bodhi" up to "the characteristic of bodhi."
This breaks the mark of bodhi.
Third, from "If Maitreya enters parinirvāṇa" down to "inducing the various devaputras," it breaks nirvāṇa.
Fourth, in reality there is no one who generates the resolve for awakening; thus,
the generation of the resolve is refuted,
and likewise, there is no one who regresses.
This refutes the practice of non-retrogression.
By abandoning the view that discriminates between [the mundane and] awakening, it further refutes the underlying basis for awakening;
this is because it clarifies that these devaputras, though their minds delight in awakening, possess much attachment to signs.
Therefore, this is again refuted.
From here on, the emptiness of bodhi is clarified;
bodhi itself is not discussed.
It is empty because it lacks intrinsic nature.
This merely clarifies that bodhi is wondrously transcendent of sensory objects;
because its essence is devoid of manifold characteristics, it is said to be empty.
This does not mean that it is non-existent.
From here below, the refutation of bodhi is clarified;
there are three parts in total.
Because it has reached the state where arising, abiding, and ceasing do not exist,
the essence of bodhi is empty.
One who abandons the view that discriminates bodhi [realizes this].
Enlightenment is luminous, wondrously transcendent, and invisible.
Why is this so? Why is it that one abandons the view of enlightenment?
"Not attained through body or mind" clarifies that bodhi is wondrously transcendent;
it is transcendent of the very substance of body and mind.
It is neither body nor mind.
What, then, is this seeing?
From "quiescent extinction" (*śānta*) onwards, there are six sections of explanation.
Regarding the statement that "initially, quiescence is bodhi because it extinguishes all marks," this generally clarifies that it is not attained by means of body or mind;
such is the characteristic of quiescence.
The second, from "Enlightenment is non-contemplation" up to "because of being without recollection," clarifies that enlightenment does not contemplate objects nor recollect objects.
The third, from "Enlightenment is cessation" downward to "because of being without attachment," [clarifies the same].
Illuminating bodhi means severing afflictions;
because one abandons all views and is free from false conceptualization,
it is said that illumination severs all views.
It obstructs all vows and is free from attachment;
it severs the five dull [afflictions].
"Vow" refers to the conceptualization of craving as a vow.

The fourth [point], "Bodhi proceeds from accordance until it reaches the limit of reality," clarifies that bodhi is devoid of manifold characteristics and its essence is identical to the three emptinesses.
The fifth, "Non-duality is bodhi," is a single phrase that resolves doubts.
The preceding section clarified that being in accord with the three emptinesses is termed bodhi;
it was called "in accord" because one takes the three emptinesses as an object.
Now, it is said that this is because one has departed from mind and dharmas.
Taking non-enlightenment as the mind and the three emptinesses as the phenomena,
it is therefore said that one is "detached from mind and phenomena."
The latter two phrases both clarify the essence of bodhi.
Regarding the second point, "knowing is bodhi because one knows the mental activities of sentient beings":
the preceding section clarified that the essence of bodhi is empty.
At that time, his mind, having sunk into expectation, returned;
he realized that bodhi exists and fully understood the mental activities of sentient beings.
The third [point], "will not be bodhi," and so forth,
clarifies bodhi above;
it refers to the time when one realizes the activities of the mind.
The passage "the mind acts with intention and grasps" serves to further clarify that bodhi is without characteristics (animitta).
This is why Guangyan said he was "incapable."
In his dialogue with the layman, the principle was somewhat obscured;

at one point, the layman said, "I have come from the *bodhimaṇḍa*, yet I do not understand that the myriad practices are also the *bodhimaṇḍa*. This refers to the place where the Buddha attained the Way as being the *bodhimaṇḍa*.
When asked by the lay follower, he said:
"One attains *sambodhi* at the various sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
One may say that one comes from the site of enlightenment; as for the reason why this is so, it is because..."
What is this so-called "site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*)?
The Buddha explains that the fruit of Buddhahood is called the site of enlightenment because one may mount it to transform sentient beings; thus, it possesses the meaning of a "path."
It can remove the false and delusive afflictions of sentient beings and give rise to their genuine understanding;
it is likened to a path because the myriad practices may be traversed toward Buddhahood, and thus it possesses the meaning of "path."
Because the myriad practices can eliminate evil and give rise to wondrous understanding, they possess the meaning of a "site" (kṣetra).
From the straightforward mind up to the truths, this is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa);
it is called the site of enlightenment by way of its cause.
The fearlessnesses are explained in terms of the Four Truths;
therefore, the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is mentioned among the external conditions.
The powers and fearlessnesses, as well as those that follow, are also explained within the context of practice.
The difference lies in the practice for the sake of the fruit.
If one accords with the practice of the various pāramitās,
then in teaching and transforming all beings, there is never a time when one does not approach the fruit accompanied by the ten thousand practices.
Therefore, it is said that they all come from the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and immediately abide in what the Buddha rides.
Now, to clarify the lifting and setting down of the feet:
the absence of marks (animitta) constitutes the lifting of the foot.
To regard the celebration of external signs as insufficient is acceptable.
To practice it oneself is the lifting of the foot; to transform others is the setting down of the foot.
Dhāraṇīdhara has lost his skill in means because he does not recognize the true [nature of things] and is unable to respond with skillful means to propagate the Dharma;
therefore, he was incapable of inquiring after the illness.
Māra knew that he had not attained [realization].
To give away one's daughter for the sake of wealth destroys the intent for the Way;
the World-Holder calls such a person Śakra.
One should constantly revile the three— body, life, and wealth.
"Releasing" means that body,
life, and wealth are constant.
Therefore, when it is said now that one should contemplate impermanence to seek the root of goodness,
it clarifies that by means of the three non-solid dharmas, one attains the three solid dharmas; thus,
it points to the non-solid as the very root of goodness.
As for "sinking is not appropriate for me," there are two kinds of inappropriateness:
first, that female beauty is what is common among householders and is not appropriate for those who have left the home life.
Second, these women’s faculties for the Path are nearly matured while they remain with Vimalakīrti;
furthermore, it would not be appropriate for me to importune them.
"To importune" means... [text continues]
This is indeed like a leak;
it is intended to cause that person to give rise to various outflows,
just as I am one who should receive them.
There are two kinds of "that which should be received":
first, because sensual desire for form is what I have practiced while living at home, it is said that it "should be received";
second, because such a person will surely receive my Dharma upon awakening, it is further said that they "should immediately receive" it.
He preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate,
subduing Māra so that he may receive transformation through him.
There is the joy of the Dharma, which clarifies that one finds delight in the Dharma for oneself.
When one shifts from prior attachment to a joyful understanding, the spirit is delighted;
therefore, it is called "Dharma-joy.
Furthermore, lower-grade wisdom, insight, and roots of goodness are all the essence of Dharma-joy.
Delighting in constant faith in the Buddha up to the extensive practice of giving,
one clearly abides in the essence of the preceding dharmas;
from the practice of giving up to the vast bodhicitta.
This sequentially clarifies the essential characteristics of the Dharma-joy within the six stages (*bhūmi*).
At the seventh stage, one first attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and is able to subdue Māra.
One abandons the two kinds of afflictions;
one practices the eight stages of dwelling in the cultivation of the pure land;
and one accomplishes the marks and signs through the nine stages of dwelling.
Delighting in adorning the site of enlightenment is the practice of the ten stages of abiding;
delighting in hearing the profound Dharma without fear of inferiority is the thorough illumination of the roots of goodness of wisdom of the three vehicles.
"Not delighting in what is not wealth" clarifies that when sentient beings should hear [the Dharma] and attain awakening, they should regard wisdom as "non-wealth.
Furthermore, it is explained thus:
When the roots of the Path are about to ripen, one does not delight in those whose roots are not yet mature;
one delights in associating with fellow students.
Because the principles of the Mahāyāna are studied by both oneself and others, they are called "fellow students."
Those whose minds are free from anger and obstruction are transformed through the teachings of the Hīnayāna so that they may follow the Mahāyāna;
those who harbor anger in their hearts [are not].
It cannot be so;
one must not protect wicked people who harm the roots of my Way.
One should protect those in the evil realms with abundant external compassion;
because that which they abide in is vast, it is necessary to protect them.
A virtuous friend is the Buddha.
Being close to them, they give rise to goodness;
